transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-08 16:00 PST
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Leah Cho (Redwood SE), Marco Ruiz (Oxidian - Lead ML Eng), Priya Nair (Oxidian - SRE), Daniel Kim (Oxidian - Product)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
- Reviewed week 2 POC bench: tail latency and 95th while increasing concurrency.
- Identified two hotspots: KV-cache cold starts and routing to smaller model variant for cheap requests.
- Agreed next steps: share CSV/logs, lab replay, and plan canary for dedicated slots if numbers hold.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: okay hey everyone, Samir here from Redwood. thanks for joining. how are we doing on time, Leah?
[00:06] Leah: yeah we've got 40-ish minutes. plan to run through the numbers, then call out tuning items and next steps.
[00:12] Marco: awesome, thanks. i pulled up the baseline numbers so we can compare side by side.
[00:18] Samir: perfect. quick reminder — this is week two of the POC. objective is to validate latency at 95th and throughput at our expected qps, and compare unit cost to Oxidian's incumbent.
[00:31] Priya: yes and also network egress patterns — we saw a spike last night that masked some of the tail, so we'll want to look at traces.
[00:40] Leah: cool, i'll share the perf deck. first slide: summary of runs we executed during 3/2–3/7. we ran 1) steady-state QPS ramp to 600, 2) bursty tail test, and 3) long-tail sequence length test at 1k tokens.
[01:02] Marco: baseline (incumbent) 95th was ~310ms with 600 qps, average around 110ms. your run shows 95th around 360.
[01:12] Samir: yep that's accurate — overall we're slightly higher on 95th in the out-of-box config, but median is much better on our runtime for longer sequences. key callouts: our KV cache warm-up wasn't optimal in the first three runs. once cache warmed up we saw the 95th drop to ~290ms in later runs.
[01:30] Marco: interesting, do you have the warm-up curve? how many parallel requests until warm cache?
[01:37] Leah: (sharing) graph 3 shows warm-up: roughly 150 concurrent distinct sessions to reach stable KV hit rate; most of your traffic pattern is session-heavy so warm-up matters.
[01:48] Priya: that explains the spike last night — a rollout from their infra created new sessions. our request mix is chatty, small prompts, so steady concurrency is lower than expected.
[01:58] Samir: okay, so two levers here: pre-warm cache during canary or use prefix caching at the app layer; and routing policy — push small, cheap requests to a quantized variant where possible.
[02:12] Daniel: about quantized variant — how much accuracy delta do you expect? we can't degrade NLU beyond a threshold.
[02:19] Leah: from our internal evals, for short prompts quantized int8 path showed — in most RAG-like prompts — less than 1.5% delta on similarity metrics. but we always recommend running your eval set.
[02:32] Marco: ok we'll run an eval set. what about throughput? we saw your 600 qps steady-state throughput saturates at 8 GPUs in your Dedicated profile; incumbent runs at 6 GPUs for same qps but with higher tail. is the difference kernel-level scheduling?
[02:48] Leah: it's a mix — our runtime chooses different kernels for longer sequences and keeps KV cache pinned. in the incumbent they rely on batched sync that can starve the KV path. effectively we trade a bit more reserved GPU for more consistent tails.
[03:03] Marco: so cost question — they're cheaper on per-hour instances but we care about per-request unit cost. did you compute per-1M tokens?
[03:11] Samir: yes. rough numbers from the run: incumbent unit cost $4.2 per 1M tokens; our initial profile $3.6 per 1M tokens after applying batching+prefix cache and routing for small prompts it drops to $2.9. note these are lab numbers excluding network egress and reserved discounts.
[03:28] Priya: are those with quantized models or fp16?
[03:31] Leah: the $2.9 includes int8 quantization on the cheap route plus prefix cache hit rates of ~42%. the $3.6 was fp16 with caching but without aggressive routing.
[03:40] Marco: hmm, so if we can get a steady 40% cache hit in prod, that looks compelling. how stable are those cache hit rates with our request skew?
[03:49] Leah: that depends; we saw variance during rolling deploys. suggestion: stabilize by using sticky session routing and shorter rolling windows during deploy.
[03:58] Daniel: network/infra note — we have tight egress limits in our VPC; will your private deployment option respect our KMS/HSM for keys?
[04:07] Samir: yes for Private we integrate with customer KMS and we can support HSM-backed signing — that's part of the enterprise package. we'll share the security pack.
[04:16] Marco: great. one other observation — tail percentiles for long sequences were better on your runtime. our application sometimes hits 1k tokens for summarization; does the runtime change kernels at 512 boundary?
[04:27] Leah: good question. yes we pick kernels based on sequence length and micro-batch. our compilation chooses an attention kernel optimized for >512 contexts; that reduces per-token compute when sequences are heavy.
[04:37] Priya: we also noticed a small number of OOMs in the 1k test with the incumbent, which caused retries. did you have any OOMs during your runs?
[04:44] Leah: in our config we didn't hit OOM; we tuned batch size and used continuous batching to avoid per-step spikes. there were some retry spikes early but they correlated with KV miss storms.
[04:55] Marco: okay, so practically, what are the immediate knobs for us to try in the next lab replay?
[05:01] Leah: we'll try 1) pre-warm KV cache via synthetic sessions for 30 minutes before the test, 2) adjust routing threshold to push <64-token prompts to quantized variant, 3) enforce sticky sessions with your load balancer settings, 4) increase min GPU slots to reduce cold-start scheduling.
[05:18] Samir: i'll package these as a runbook and drop the exact commands. also we'll include the change to autoscaling to avoid aggressive scale-in during bursts.
[05:27] Marco: do you have a recommended canary size if we want to mirror production? our prod footprint is ~2k rps peak.
[05:34] Leah: for traffic-safety i'd recommend a 2% canary of your peak, so around 40 rps, run for 48 hours while we compare traces and error rates. if that looks good we can step to 10% for another 48 hours.
[05:47] Priya: timeline-wise — we need these numbers to be ready for our internal security review on 3/22.
[05:54] Samir: understood. we'll aim to run the lab replay next week, share raw CSVs by 3/10 so you have time for review.
[06:01] Daniel: about the raw CSVs — include per-request latencies, trace id, node id, and whether it was routed to quantized path.
[06:09] Leah: will do. and we'll add a column for KV-cache hit/miss and sequence length.
[06:15] Marco: can you also annotate which runs included warm-up vs cold start? that's important for our SLA model.
[06:21] Samir: yes — every run will have a metadata row.
[06:24] (brief pause while Samir types a note)
[06:30] Marco: side question — any concerns with our incumbent contract termination? they have a 60-day clause but may charge termination fees, just flagging.
[06:38] Samir: noted. that's more commercial — i'll loop in our account team but for performance we've tried to focus on the tech parallel.
[06:44] Priya: ok acceptance criteria for us: 95th at or below incumbent within 10% and unit cost at least 15% lower net of egress.
[06:54] Leah: fair. that's achievable with the knobs we discussed; lab replay will prove viability.
[07:00] Marco: any other blockers?
[07:03] Samir: just the traces and baseline config from you; once we have that we'll run the replay and share the notebook/CSV.
[07:10] Daniel: sounds good. let's capture next steps.
[07:13] Samir: recap: Samir share CSV + runbook by 3/10; Leah schedule lab replay and invite Priya for the networking checks week of 3/15; Marco send incumbent config and traces by 3/11; Daniel confirm canary stakeholders by 3/12.
[07:30] Marco: thanks everyone. i think this is productive.
[07:33] Priya: thanks.
[07:35] Leah: thanks all, we'll follow up in thread.
[07:37] Samir: bye everyone.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription: speaker labels may be approximate; some proper nouns could be mis-transcribed (e.g., kernel names). Refer to attached perf CSV and raw logs for authoritative numbers.
